title: Run the application on a VPS
summary: Supply Boot configuration to a dedicated Java process and let systemd manage its lifecycle.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: How to Host Spring Boot on VPS: Production Guide (2026)

richText: A Boot process on a VPS
A VPS runs the same executable JAR described in the packaging lesson.
The installed Java runtime must support the application’s compiled Java version.
External properties provide database connections, credentials, profiles, and server settings.
A dedicated operating-system account runs the application. It needs access to its JAR and required files, rather than administrative privileges.
Process management
On a Linux host using systemd, a service unit defines how the Boot process starts and stops.
systemd can start that process at boot and restart it after failure.
The Java process writes normal console logs to the service demo unless other logging is configured.
A service start can succeed before Boot finishes starting. An application request checks readiness after startup.
A systemd service

example.title: Run the demo JAR as a managed service
description: Java `17` and Maven are required. The files form a separate project rooted at `pom.xml`.
The Linux host uses systemd and Java `17` at `/usr/bin/java`. The `demo` account and group already exist.
The commands run on the host from the project root. `/opt/demo` already exists. The service account can read its JAR but cannot replace it.
The root-owned `/etc/demo.env` file has restricted permissions. The two absolute-path tabs show host configuration files.
Each host configuration tab is saved at its displayed absolute path before the service commands run.
explanation: `EnvironmentFile` passes its environment variables to Java. Boot maps the server variables to `server.address` and `server.port`.
`WorkingDirectory` also determines the base for relative application file paths.
`ExecStart` runs the executable JAR as the `demo` account.
`Restart=on-failure` retries a failed process after five seconds.
`TimeoutStopSec` gives the process time to stop before systemd forces termination.
`daemon-reload` reads the changed unit. `enable --now` starts it and enables startup at boot.
`journalctl` shows the application’s console logs. Startup failures appear there.
example.commands:
mvn clean package
sudo install -o root -g demo -m 640 target/demo.jar /opt/demo/demo.jar
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now demo.service
sudo systemctl restart demo.service
systemctl status demo.service
journalctl -u demo.service -n 100 --no-pager
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/

files.name: src/main/java/com/example/demo/DemoApplication.java
src/main/java/com/example/demo/GreetingController.java
/etc/systemd/system/demo.service
files.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/demo.service
[Unit]
Description=Demo application
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=demo
Group=demo
WorkingDirectory=/opt/demo
EnvironmentFile=/etc/demo.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/demo/demo.jar
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
TimeoutStopSec=60
NoNewPrivileges=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

richText: Startup and shutdown
A repeated restart can mean a missing property, an incompatible Java runtime, a port conflict, or an unavailable dependency. The application log identifies the actual failure.
Boot
c
enables graceful shutdown for its embedded servers by default.
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase
c
sets the grace period. The service manager’s stop timeout must allow that work to finish.
A service restart after installing a new JAR starts new application classes. Replacing the file alone does not update the running process.
Releases
The deployed JAR needs an identifiable application revision and a retained prior artifact for rollback.
After a restart, startup logs and a controlled application request check the new release.
Database migrations and backups need their own plan. Rolling back the JAR does not roll back database changes.
